title: A share that only grows
question: Which payees took a larger share of one department’s outside spending in at least six of the seven years since fiscal 2019?
finding: 2,641 payee-and-department pairs were paid in every one of the eight years; in 46 of them (1.7%) the payee’s share rose in six or seven of the seven year-to-year steps. Chance alone would give about 165, so a share that climbs without pause is rarer than a coin toss would make it, not commoner. The test can turn on a move of a few hundredths of a point, so a pair is listed only if it also meets the test when each payment is counted in the year the file lists it under: 30 pairs meet it both ways. 13 of the 30 were paid $500,000 or more in fiscal 2026: Bar Association Of San Francisco at Superior Court (10.2% to 16.7%, $772,079 to $1.0 million); Moffatt & Nichol at Recreation & Park Commission (0.0% to 5.5%, $18,545 to $3.3 million); Community Youth Center San Francisco at Children, Youth & Families (2.9% to 5.9%, $2.4 million to $6.6 million). 2 of the 13 have nothing recorded as competed and 6 carry a warning sign elsewhere in this project.
how: For every department with at least $5 million of outside spending in each year, each payee’s payments are divided by the department’s outside spending that year, fiscal 2019 to 2026; a payment belongs to the year its voucher was issued in, read from the voucher number. A pair is listed when the payee was paid in all eight years, its share rose in at least six of the seven steps and ended above where it began, and it was paid $500,000 or more in fiscal 2026. The pair must also meet the same test when each payment is counted in the fiscal year the file lists it under; the figures shown are by the year of issue. "How awarded" reads the purchasing rule keyed on the payee’s payments from that department over the eight years. The chance figure is the number of pairs times 8/128, the odds of six or seven rises in seven even tosses. Ranked by the gain in share.
limits: A growing share can mean a growing need: a construction firm midway through one large project, a provider asked to open more sites, a landlord whose rent rises on schedule. A share also rises when the department’s other spending falls. Incumbents can also keep winning where the service is specialised, the same clients need continuity of care, few providers qualify, or one multi-year contract spans the whole period. What would settle each row: the solicitation and scoring sheets behind the awards that made the share grow, or the sole-source justification where there was none. 43 pairs meet the test under only one of the two ways of dating a payment (16 by the year the voucher was issued, 27 by the year the file lists it under) and are not listed; for 11 of them the payee’s own yearly dollars are the same either way and only the department’s total moved. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days. The $992.6 million of outside spending that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier is in none of the figures here; it is used only to tell that a payee is not new.
